item.title: Daily Steps: Science Debunks 10,000-Step Myth
item.description:
The 10,000-Step Goal Was Never Based on Science: Here’s What Research Actually Shows

Debunking a Global Fitness Phenomenon

For decades, the 10,000-step daily goal has become ubiquitous in fitness culture, featured prominently on smartwatches, fitness trackers, and health apps worldwide. It’s promoted by health organizations, adopted by corporate wellness programs, and has become the default target for millions seeking to improve their health through increased physical activity. Yet a major new scientific study has revealed a startling truth: this widely accepted benchmark has virtually no scientific foundation. The 10,000-step figure, it turns out, was born not from rigorous medical research but from a 1960s Japanese marketing campaign for a pedometer called the “Manpo-keri,” which translates to “10,000 steps meter.”

item.title: Earth Microbes Survive Moon Shadows
item.description:
Earth Microbes Survive Moon Shadows

NASA-led modeling in Science Advances finds that human-associated bacteria and fungi could survive days in shaded niches near the lunar south pole, including Artemis III candidate sites. The work is not a claim that Earth life is already blooming on the Moon. It is a claim about survival, in shade, for days, in places crews may soon walk. Using Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter maps of Nobile Rim, Connecting Ridge, and De Gerlache Rim, researchers tested organisms common on skin and spacecraft such as Aspergillus niger, Bacillus subtilis, and Deinococcus radiodurans. Survivable pockets ranged from crater floors to boot-print scale. Hardy Aspergillus resisted UV enough to persist even with some sunlight, up to about a week in places.

item.title: Cancer CAR-T Puts Arthritis In Remission
item.description:
Cancer CAR-T Puts Arthritis In Remission

Charité researchers in Berlin tested CD19 CAR T-cell therapy in six people with severe, treatment-refractory rheumatoid arthritis, the world’s first such trial, ScienceDaily reported from a Nature Medicine paper dated Aug. 29. The work does not introduce a new daily pill. It takes a living-cell treatment built for cancer and asks whether the same hunt for CD19-marked B cells can quiet a joint disease that had already outlasted as many as eight targeted or biologic therapies over a decade.

item.title: Roman Telescope Launches Sunday Morning
item.description:
Roman Telescope Launches Sunday Morning

NASA’s $4.3 billion Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is targeted for 7:26 a.m. EDT Sunday, Aug. 30, on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy from Kennedy Space Center pad 39A. The time is a clock time, not a slogan. A flagship observatory is on a heavy-lift rocket on Florida’s Space Coast, Space Force weather officers have put favorable conditions at 60 percent, and the next great NASA sky survey is scheduled to leave Earth before breakfast on the East Coast.

item.title: AI Maps Six Hidden Earth Structures
item.description:
AI Maps Six Hidden Earth Structures

About 1,800 miles beneath your feet, Earth’s mantle meets the liquid outer core. That contact is not a smooth seam. It is a landscape. For decades seismologists have known that the base of the mantle is lumpy, with patches of odd material that scatter passing earthquake waves. Mapping those patches has always been a fight against faint signals and uneven coverage. A new effort from Chinese Academy of Sciences researchers uses a deep-learning system, a mountain of old seismograms, and a lot of human cleanup to argue that the lumps are more connected, and more numerous, than earlier catalogs showed.

item.title: Frozen Frogs Restart After Hearts Stop
item.description:
Frozen Frogs Restart After Hearts Stop

A North American wood frog can spend winter looking dead and still hop away in spring. That sentence sounds like folklore, the kind of campfire claim that dissolves under a thermometer. It is not folklore. It is a seasonal, whole-body freeze, and it is one of the starkest survival tricks still operating in temperate forests. Ice forms. The animal stiffens. Heartbeat, breathing, and obvious brain activity stop. Then, months later, the same frog thaws in a sequence that is closer to a restart protocol than to a simple melt, and it walks back into a world of meltwater and insects.

item.title: Shark Graveyard Found in Egyptian Desert
item.description:
Shark Graveyard Found in Egyptian Desert

The Western Desert of Egypt is a place of wind and phosphate, not of surf. About 80 million years ago it was a shallow inland sea. Paleontologists led by Cairo University’s Tarek Yassin have now pulled 14 fossil shark teeth from phosphate beds on the Abu-Tartur Plateau, and those teeth are enough to redraw a local roster of Cretaceous hunters. The find is being called a shark “graveyard,” with the scare quotes doing honest work. It is not a single pile of animals that died together. It is a seafloor archive from a mixed, nutrient-rich Tethys margin, later lifted into desert as the sea retreated.
